content: Utilization behavior is a neurological condition associated with frontal lobe dysfunction. Patients with this disorder exhibit an inability to suppress the urge to interact with or use objects that are within their visual field and physical reach. This behavior is not merely impulsive; rather, patients often provide fabricated or confabulated explanations to justify their actions, which distinguishes it from other impulse-control disorders. The phenomenon was extensively studied by Lhermitte in 1983, who explored its connection to frontal lobe lesions. His research, published in Brain (Volume 106, Pages 237–255), highlighted the critical role of the frontal lobes in regulating autonomous behavior. In a subsequent study in 1986, Lhermitte further examined the implications of frontal lobe dysfunction on human autonomy, particularly in complex and social contexts. He introduced the concept of environmental dependency syndrome, which describes the tendency of patients to rely excessively on environmental cues to guide their behavior, often leading to inappropriate or automatic actions. This work was detailed in Annals of Neurology.
